title: Teaching the bass: quarter notes, tone choice and individuality
summary: He explains the bassist as timekeeper, choosing tones, and improvisation as adding, removing or leaving things, which he teaches students.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You found the groove. Yeah. Speaking of groove, I wanted to talk a little bit more about, you spoke so eloquently about Paul Chambers and responsibility of notes, and the quarter notes. And I’m trying to form a question here that has something to do with a combination of where you put the quarter notes and what pitches you chooses to play when.
What pitches I use to play —
What pitches you choose to play on what beats and getting from one chord to the next. I don’t really have a question here, Cecil, but —

No I hear you. I hear a question. I’m actually teaching this quite favorably. I’m actually excited about a couple of students I’m teaching, these technique to. You asked me before do I teach them how to play — teach them what to play. I don’t teach them what to play, I give them information as to be capable, to provide that they would be capable in any situation. And see fundamentally the bass player soloing, that is the reward of the effort, the previous efforts, that is to understand that your function, you’re the timekeeper. The pronouncement of that quarter note, given one-two-three-four — the pronouncement of that quarter note is very essential, that not only that it’s pronounced exactly on the beat but that it expands when it’s played only to blend in with the next tone on the second or third beat. Right? So that keeps the time. And even directs the functions of various harmonies that would prevail at the time. The main thing is as a young kid coming along, this is your fundamental reality, that you’re the timekeeper and you know, accented by your choices of qualities of tone. Now qualities of tones reference of course the current scale of the current chord, given your choices of tones as you proceed from situation to situation. I mean really if you know what you’re doing and you understand what the science of that is, that provides, uniquely for the most part, individuality. Because as you

choose that tone you are the one that made that decision at that time for that purpose, given how you feel about the moment. Now if you want to, like I did earlier, every now and then infuse something that Paul did, that’s all good as a learning experience, but as you grow and mature then individuality should prevail because you know more of what you’re doing to the extent that you can make unique individual choices. Because see this music that we are excited about in this world is about improvisation of course. Improvisation is about adding something to a given situation, removing something from a given situation, or leaving it — letting it stand entirely. And sometimes that can be in motion or when you’re standing still. You can lay the bar lines down and fashion various progressions that way. So how you, the choice that you make in terms of your reducing something or adding something, you know, as things are progressing, that provides individuality given the extent of your study, which you would provide awareness of really what you’re doing. So this is what I’m teaching these guys you know. It’s not about you’ve got a tune, it’s not what you should play it’s the excitement of choices that you make at the moment as you go from situation to situation. I teach that playing is about a series of crescendos from left to right. It’s about arriving and departing from situations. As you arrive to a situation you are actually leaving a situation simultaneously. There is where the uniqueness of individuality is, the choice that you make at that moment. Leaving and departing and arriving and departing, you see?
Those are some very quotable statements, Cecil.
